title: Types of clay targets
summary: Standard, midi, mini, battue, rabbit, flash, ZZ and rocket: how the targets differ, how they fly, and why the menu names each special target.

body.html: A target, often called a “clay”, is a brittle disc thrown by a machine called a trap. Knowing the type of target helps you plan the shot before you call.
The battue flies edge-on, then turns over and drops; the rabbit rolls along the ground.
body.heading: Watch how the target flies

body.html: The FITASC list for Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ names seven target types: standard, midi, super mini, battue, rabbit, flash and ZZ. Compak® Sporting allows any standard or special target, and its list also names the rocket. Each type flies differently.

The standard, the most common target, is a dome about 108–110 mm across; beginners usually start on it. The midi is 90 mm: it keeps its speed well and looks further away than it is. The mini is usually 60 mm: it leaves the trap fast and slows quickly. So shooters tend to give it too much lead, that is, they shoot too far in front of it. Names of small targets vary: the Sporting™ list says “super mini”, and menus may show 70 mm or 60 mm. Go by the millimetres written on the menu.

The battue is a flat, thin 110 mm target. It flies edge-on, almost invisible, then turns to show its face and drops quickly. The Compak® Sporting rules advise against battues on very short trajectories. The rabbit is a 110 mm target with a thick, strong rim, rolled on its edge along the ground; it bounces and can hop over bumps. See also The rabbit: rolling, hopping and bolting.

A flash target is filled with coloured powder that leaves a bright cloud when it is hit; it is scored like any other target. A ZZ target, also called helice, is a plastic propeller with a white centre cap that flies erratically. The rocket is another special target, named only in the Compak® Sporting list.
In Sporting™ the target menu in front of each shooting stand (the spot you shoot from) must name any special targets: 90 mm, 70 mm or 60 mm, battue or rabbit. Read it before you step onto the stand.
In Sporting™, a target of the wrong colour, size or type is a No Bird (the target does not count) and is thrown again.
Colour is not a type of target: it is chosen so that the target stands out against the background. See Colours, light and visibility.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The midi looks far but it isn't — don't give it too much.
phrases.meaning: The coach's correction for this target: it looks further away than it is, so this shooter is giving it more lead (more distance in front) than it needs. It is a correction for this situation, not a general rule.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The battue will turn and drop at the end — take it when it shows its belly.
phrases.meaning: Shoot the battue once it turns its flat face towards you.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The mini is dying fast — shoot it early.
phrases.meaning: The small target loses speed quickly; do not wait.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The rabbit will hop on that bump — stay under it.
phrases.meaning: Keep the gun pointed low on the rolling target, so that if it hops up it jumps into the shot.

key_points.html: Standard about 108–110 mm, midi 90 mm, mini usually 60 mm; the menu may also show 70 mm, so go by the millimetres.
Battue: flat, edge-on, turns and drops; rabbit: thick rim, rolls and hops.
Flash leaves a powder cloud; ZZ is a propeller target.
Sporting™ list: standard, midi, super mini, battue, rabbit, flash, ZZ; Compak® Sporting allows any type, rocket included.
Sporting™: wrong colour, size or type = No Bird.

did_you_know.html: A mini looks easy because it is small, but many shooters find it one of the trickiest: it starts very fast and then suddenly slows down.

quiz.q: What size is a mini target usually?
quiz.explain: A mini is usually 60 mm and a midi 90 mm. Names of small targets vary, so go by the millimetres on the menu.

quiz.q: On a Sporting™ stand, a trap throws a midi instead of the standard shown on the menu. What happens?

options.text: No Bird, the target is repeated

quiz.explain: In Sporting™ a target of the wrong colour, size or type is a No Bird (it does not count) and is thrown again.

quiz.q: Which target rolls along the ground?
quiz.explain: The rabbit has a thick rim and is thrown on its edge along the ground.
